transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-02-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Lucas (Redwood SE), Samira (DataHarbor Head of ML), Ethan (DataHarbor Infra), Priya (DataHarbor SRE)
---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um quick intros then we can jump in. i'm maya from redwood, lucas is our se.
[00:12] Samira: hi all, samira here, thanks - excited to scope the benchmark POC.
[00:17] Lucas: thanks, couple goals today - align on success criteria, what your scripts look like, and timeline for a load run.
[00:30] Ethan: yeah we want to validate both streaming and non-streaming inference; production targets are 500 qps peak, p50 < 60ms, p95 < 250ms, and cost below $0.0008/token roughly.
[01:05] Priya: also security: must be VPC-only for the pilot, kms for keys, audit logs and SSO integration.
[01:28] Maya: good, that's helpful. on success criteria, we usually split perf (latency/throughput), stability (error rates, mem OOMs), and quality/regression checks against your eval prompts.
[01:52] Samira: for quality we have a holdout set of 2k prompts; for perf we have a mix: 70% short queries (~32 tokens), 20% medium (~128), 10% long (~512).
[02:15] Lucas: perfect. for harness integration, do you have existing load scripts? are they in locust/jmeter/custom python?
[02:30] Ethan: we have a custom python harness that wraps their client and streams tokens for some flows; it's a bit bespoke but we can definitely package it.
[02:46] Maya: ok good - we can ingest customer scripts into our benchmark harness. two things to call out: streaming tests measure token-level latency and are more sensitive to network jitter; non-streaming tests measure end-to-end response times. both are useful.
[03:10] Samira: can you explain how redwood handles prefix caching / kv cache? we rely on a lot of repeated context.
[03:28] Lucas: yeah so we have automatic prefix caching and KV cache persistence for active sessions; note that during pure load tests caching can artificially improve p50 if the dataset has many repeats. we'll instrument cache hits in the harness. (laugh)
[03:53] Ethan: is cache behaviour configurable for the run? we want to see both cold-cache and warm-cache scenarios.
[04:05] Lucas: absolutely - we can run cold-start passes and warm-start passes. we'll capture cache hit metrics and show token count breakdown.
[04:25] Priya: network: for VPC setup, will we need a peering or can you access our private cluster via a temporary agent?
[04:39] Maya: for private deployments we typically use a customer-managed VPC peering; for the pilot we can do a short-lived tunnel or deploy the harness inside your VPC (SE to confirm).
[04:58] Lucas: i'd prefer deploying the harness in your VPC so we remove network variability; we'll send an infra checklist.
[05:16] Samira: timeline wise, we'd like initial results by the end of next week if possible. is that realistic?
[05:26] Maya: depends on how fast we get scripts and sample data; if we get those in 48-72 hours, se can spin up a test cluster and run smoke tests in 5 business days.
[05:40] Samira: ok we'll prioritize.
[05:46] Ethan: on the model side, are you suggesting specific model variants or quantization? we use 8-bit for cost efficiency in prod sometimes.
[05:59] Lucas: we'll recommend a couple of variants: an FP16 variant to baseline perf, and a quantized variant to measure cost/perf tradeoffs. we'll include guidance on tokenizer and sequence length to mirror your workload.
[06:20] Samira: what about streaming vs non-streaming—do you see big differences?
[06:30] Lucas: yes, streaming tends to show lower p50 because partial tokens arrive early, but total tokens and p95 may vary. also batching behaviour is different: streaming requests often can't be batched as aggressively without adding latency.
[06:52] Priya: we need clear SLO definitions. p50/p95 token latency, and also a tail latency budget for 99th percentile if possible.
[07:06] Maya: noted. we'll add p99 as an optional metric but focus p50/p95 as your primary.
[07:18] Samira: for accuracy/regression, do you run evals inside the harness or separately?
[07:28] Lucas: we can wire your eval set into the same harness; after each run we calculate quality deltas and flag regressions. it's part of our standard POC package.
[07:45] Ethan: on concurrency, to hit 500 qps with average latency ~100ms, we'd need around 50 concurrent streams, correct?
[07:59] Lucas: ballpark yes, depends on sequence length distribution and batching; we'll simulate realistic concurrency based on your sample traces.
[08:13] Samira: we'll share traces of production traffic (anonymized).
[08:22] Maya: great. let's talk artifacts—what we need from you: (1) sample prompts (~5k or less), (2) your custom harness scripts, (3) any auth details to access a test VPC or deploy an agent, (4) target success criteria doc.
[08:44] Priya: i'll own the VPC/network checklist and send it.
[08:49] Ethan: i'll package the harness and a small dataset.
[08:55] Samira: i'll write the success criteria doc and share.
[09:02] Lucas: on the redwood side we'll: provision a temporary dedicated pool for the pilot, import your harness, run cold/warm cache runs, streaming and non-streaming passes, and provide a report with latency histograms, throughput curves, cost estimates and a regression table.
[09:27] Maya: rough schedule: get artifacts by 2027-02-13, lucas to run smoke tests by 2027-02-19, full runs week of 2027-02-21, results delivered 2027-02-25.
[09:45] Samira: that works. any blockers re: compliance? we need SOC2 report and MFA on access.
[09:55] Maya: we can share our SOC2 and security whitepaper; SE will follow up with the attestation and the minimum access roles required.
[10:07] Priya: also curious about data retention: will any customer data be persisted on redwood logs?
[10:18] Lucas: by default logs are generated for metrics only; we can disable request logging or ensure logs are scrubbed. we also support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest.
[10:33] Ethan: for the harness, do you require any code changes to our scripts to be compatible?
[10:42] Lucas: usually just small adapter code to call our client or a simple wrapper; we can accept a dockerized harness too.
[10:54] Samira: about cost estimation, you mentioned cost per token earlier—can you provide a rough delta between FP16 and quantized?
[11:05] Lucas: rough rule: quantized often reduces per-token cost by 30-50% depending on model and hardware; we'll provide model-specific numbers after initial runs.
[11:20] Maya: i'll include a cost worksheet in the benchmark template.
[11:28] Samira: can you run both streaming and non-streaming in same test run or separate?
[11:36] Lucas: separate runs are cleaner because the harness needs to toggle streaming headers and batching; we can automate both sequentially.
[11:49] Ethan: for the streaming tests, what client do you recommend—websocket or HTTP chunked?
[11:58] Lucas: websocket is preferred for stable token streaming; HTTP chunked works but may add variability from the proxy. we'll support both though.
[12:12] Priya: are you able to show token-level traces? we want per-token latency breakdowns.
[12:20] Lucas: yes that's part of the instrumentation; we'll output token-level timing, KV cache hits, batch sizes, and server-side queue times.
[12:33] Maya: ok sounds good. any final risks we should call out?
[12:39] Samira: main risk is network variability if harness isn't inside our vpc; also quantized model regressions on quality.
[12:50] Lucas: we'll quantify both: run cold network and in-vpc tests and include quality delta thresholds.
[13:02] Maya: recap then: deliverables and owners as discussed. we'll share the benchmark template and infra checklist today.
[13:16] Samira: yep, thanks.
[13:20] Maya: one more thing — for reporting, do you want raw logs or a summarized dashboard?
[13:28] Priya: dashboard please, plus access to raw traces if needed.
[13:34] Lucas: ok we'll prepare a results dashboard and a zip of raw traces.
[13:41] Maya: great. last checks—permissions, MFA, attestation. lucas will follow up on attestation and se will request minimal roles.
[13:52] Ethan: fine.
[13:55] Samira: thanks all, appreciate it.
[14:00] Maya: thanks everyone — meeting ended.
